footer: Records made with this tool do not guarantee legal effect. If you need an accredited timestamp (certified by Japan's Minister of Internal Affairs and Communications), please use an accredited provider.
h1: Record "when I published it" on a third-party ledger
lead: Send only the hash (fingerprint) of a text, photo or page and get a timestamp record. Your content is never uploaded. Free, no sign-up.
step1: 1. Choose a text or a file
ph_text: Paste text here (hashed inside your browser)
err_hash: Choose a text or file first.
err_rate: Rate limit reached. Please try again later.
how1: Your browser computes the SHA-256 and only the hash is sent. We never store your text or files. If you enter a page URL, our server fetches that public page once, keeps only its hashes and the URL (never shown publicly), and discards the content.
how2: You immediately get a signed time stamp (RFC 3161) from this service.
how3: It is also sent to OpenTimestamps public calendars and is anchored in a Bitcoin block within hours. After that it can be verified from the Bitcoin ledger alone, even if this service disappears.
faq1a: It is one piece of evidence on a third-party ledger that data matching this hash existed at the recorded time. It does not show that the content is true or who made it.
faq2a: No. Hashing happens inside your browser.
faq3q: What if I edit the article?
faq3a: Any change alters the hash, so record each revision (the WordPress plugin does it automatically).
st_pending: Accepted; waiting to be anchored in a Bitcoin block (usually within hours)
st_tsa_only: Signed time stamp only (Bitcoin submission being retried)
c_dl_note: Keep these; they let you verify without this service.
c_badge_note: Optional. The image is loaded from datesealed.com, so a visitor's browser contacts our server (see the Terms). The text version below loads nothing.
c_notfound: No record found for this ID.
v_lead: Choose data (a file or text) to look for records with the same hash. If you have .tsr / .ots files you can verify them too.
a_lead: An HTTP API that takes only a hash. No authentication; limited to 10/hour and 50/day per IP.
terms.what_p: DateSealed attaches a signed time stamp (RFC 3161) and a Bitcoin-ledger record (OpenTimestamps) to a SHA-256 hash that you send. It is a free tool operated by Lightscend Co., Ltd.
terms.not_p: A record is one piece of evidence that data matching the hash existed at the recorded time. It does not show that the content is true, who created it, or who holds the rights. Records made with this tool do not guarantee legal effect. If you need an accredited timestamp (certified by Japan's Minister of Internal Affairs and Communications), please use an accredited provider.
terms.store_h: What we store, and what we do not
terms.store_p: We store the hash, the record time, the signature serial number and the proof files (.tsr / .ots). If you use page URL input, we also keep the URL you entered (never shown on public pages) and the dates the page states about itself; the fetched content itself is discarded. We never receive or store your text, files or photos.
terms.ban_p: Automated bulk submission, interference with the service, and use intended to deceive others are not allowed. We may apply limits without notice.
terms.disc_p: The service is provided free, as is, and may change or end. Once a record is anchored in the Bitcoin ledger it can still be verified if this service closes.
terms.contact_p: Lightscend Co., Ltd. For questions, deletion requests or anything else, use the contact form linked in the footer.
api_note: The API reference is in English.
url_hint: We fetch the public page once and record two hashes: its main text and its raw HTML. The page content is discarded after hashing.
kind_url-text: Main-text hash of a web page
kind_url-raw: Raw-bytes hash of a web page
c_claims_h: Dates stated by the page itself
c_claims_note: Reference only. These are what the page claims about itself; DateSealed does not verify them.
terms.analytics_p: To count visits to our public pages we use Google Tag Manager and Google Analytics. Consent for cookies and advertising features is denied by default, so these tools run without setting cookies. They are not loaded on record pages (the addresses that contain a record ID) or in the API. Google may receive your IP address and the address of the page you view as part of this measurement.
fix_translation: Found an awkward translation? Help us fix it.
dg_h: How it works, at a glance
dg_1_d: A text, a photo or a web page. It stays with you.
dg_2_d: Your browser makes a 64-character fingerprint (SHA-256). Only this is sent.
dg_3b_d: Within hours, anchored in a Bitcoin block (OpenTimestamps).
dg_4_d: Download the proof files and check them yourself. Once anchored in Bitcoin, this works even if DateSealed disappears.
st_h1: Record your photo and stamp the date on it
st_lead: Choose photos. Each original is recorded (only its hash is sent; nothing is uploaded), then a copy with a small DateSealed badge is made in your browser.
st_note: The record is for your ORIGINAL file. The stamped copy is a different file (its metadata is removed too), so keep the original: it is what shows that you had the photo first. The badge can be cropped out; it points to the record page and is not proof by itself.
st_err_file: Please choose an image (JPEG, PNG or WebP).
st_err_limit: Limit reached. Please try again later; the photos done so far can be downloaded.
terms.logs_p: When you create a record, verify one, look up a hash, or use the photo stamp or the WordPress plugin, we log the time, the kind of use, the result, the IP address, the host name of that address (reverse DNS), the country and network operator it belongs to, your browser's user-agent and language settings, the language of the page you were on, and the ID of the record involved. The country and network are looked up in a database on our own server; your IP address is not sent to anyone for this. We use these logs to prevent abuse and apply rate limits, to investigate problems, and to produce usage statistics. They are not used for advertising, and they are not sold or handed to third parties except where the law requires. We keep the IP address, host name, user-agent and language settings on our server for 30 days. After that they are moved to a storage device managed by the operator at a separate site and kept there for up to 13 months. After 13 months the last part of the IP address is removed (the last 8 bits of an IPv4 address, the last 80 bits of an IPv6 address) and the rest is kept only for statistics. Counts by country, language and kind of use contain no IP address and are kept without a time limit. To ask about this data, contact us.
terms.badge_p: If a website shows the DateSealed badge image, the visitor's browser loads it from our server. For each such request we log the time, the IP address, the host name, the user-agent, and the address of the page that shows the badge (without the part after “?”), and we keep these as described under “Usage logs”. We use them to see where the badge is shown and for statistics. If you put the badge on your own site, please mention this in your privacy policy as needed.
terms.cookie_p: The public pages and the API set no cookies. (The operator's own admin screen uses a session cookie; visitors never see it.)
terms.changes_p: 2026-11-03: added “Usage logs” and “The image badge”. Until then this page said that IP addresses were kept only as salted hashes for 30 days and then deleted. Logging as described above started on the day this change was published; earlier requests were not logged this way.
